## The potential cognitive risk

- The world is more unequal than at any point since World War II
- Yet mass demand for redistribution has *not* risen to match [(Why?)]{.fragment .red}

::: {.fragment}

> **Economic inequality**: The uneven distribution of wealth (e.g., [income]{.red}) among individuals or groups within a society.

:::

::: {.incremental .fragment}

- **What** environment are we actually living in?
- **How** does living in an unequal society shape citizens' minds?
- **What if** exposure to inequality becomes unavoidable?

:::

::: {.notes}

Roadmap for the talk: three linked questions, two countries (US + China), one claim: inequality changes minds toward indifference and even conservatism, not toward demand for redistribution.

:::


# What environment?

Objective inequality vs. perceived inequality

## Are we living in an (economically) unequal world?

How do you know?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

*Common measures*

- S80/S20 Ratio: The richest 20% / the poorest 20%
- Palma Ratio: The richest 10% / the poorest 40%
- [Gini Coefficient:]{.fragment .highlight-red} The cumulative percentage of total income / the cumulative percentage of the population, starting from the poorest

:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/gini.gif){fig-align="center" height=400}

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Each measure looks at a different slice of the distribution, which is exactly why they can disagree about the same society.

:::

## Illustration

```{r}
#| label: fakeData

create_society_from_quintiles <- function(
  quintile_shares,
  n_population = 1000,
  total_income = 50000000
) {
  # Check that quintile shares sum to 1 (or 100 if in percentage)
  if (sum(quintile_shares) > 1.1) {
    quintile_shares <- quintile_shares / 100
  }
  if (abs(sum(quintile_shares) - 1) > 0.01) {
    stop("Quintile shares must sum to 1 or 100.")
  }

  # Calculate income for each quintile
  quintile_incomes <- total_income * quintile_shares

  # Number of people per quintile
  n_per_quintile <- n_population / 5

  # Calculate average income within each quintile
  avg_incomes_per_quintile <- quintile_incomes / n_per_quintile

  # Generate individual incomes with some random noise around the quintile average
  income_data <- c()
  for (i in 1:5) {
    # Generate incomes from a normal distribution centered on the quintile's average
    quintile_group_incomes <- rnorm(
      n = n_per_quintile,
      mean = avg_incomes_per_quintile[i],
      sd = avg_incomes_per_quintile[i] * 0.15
    )
    # Ensure no income is negative
    quintile_group_incomes[
      quintile_group_incomes < 0
    ] <- avg_incomes_per_quintile[i] * 0.1
    income_data <- c(income_data, quintile_group_incomes)
  }

  return(round(income_data))
}

# Source: Approximate data from World Bank/OECD
quintiles_slovenia <- c(0.093, 0.139, 0.175, 0.224, 0.369) # Low Inequality
quintiles_usa <- c(0.036, 0.088, 0.141, 0.226, 0.509) # Medium Inequality
quintiles_safrica <- c(0.025, 0.051, 0.092, 0.179, 0.653) # High Inequality

# Data for the low inequality society (modeled on Slovenia)
income_low <- create_society_from_quintiles(quintiles_slovenia)

# Data for the medium inequality society (modeled on the USA)
income_medium <- create_society_from_quintiles(quintiles_usa)

# Data for the high inequality society (modeled on South Africa)
income_high <- create_society_from_quintiles(quintiles_safrica)

# --- Step 2: Create a function to calculate all measures ---

calculate_metrics <- function(income, society_name) {
  # Gini Coefficient
  gini <- ineq(income, type = "Gini")

  # Sort income to find quantiles
  income_sorted <- sort(income)
  n <- length(income_sorted)

  # Palma Ratio (Top 10% share / Bottom 40% share)
  income_top10_share <- sum(income_sorted[floor(n * 0.9):n]) /
    sum(income_sorted)
  income_bottom40_share <- sum(income_sorted[1:floor(n * 0.4)]) /
    sum(income_sorted)
  palma <- income_top10_share / income_bottom40_share

  # S80/S20 Ratio (Top 20% total income / Bottom 20% total income)
  income_top20 <- sum(income_sorted[floor(n * 0.8):n])
  income_bottom20 <- sum(income_sorted[1:floor(n * 0.2)])
  s80_s20 <- income_top20 / income_bottom20

  # Return a data frame
  data.frame(
    Society = society_name,
    Gini = gini,
    Palma = palma,
    S80_S20 = s80_s20
  )
}

# Calculate metrics for each society
metrics_low <- calculate_metrics(income_low, "Low Inequality")
metrics_medium <- calculate_metrics(income_medium, "Medium Inequality")
metrics_high <- calculate_metrics(income_high, "High Inequality")

# Combine into a single data frame
all_metrics <- bind_rows(metrics_low, metrics_medium, metrics_high)

# --- Step 3: Visualize the results with ggplot2 ---

# First, visualize the income distributions
income_df <- data.frame(
  Income = c(income_low, income_medium, income_high),
  Society = factor(
    rep(
      c("Low Inequality", "Medium Inequality", "High Inequality"),
      each = 1000
    ),
    levels = c("Low Inequality", "Medium Inequality", "High Inequality")
  )
)

# Now, prepare data for comparing the inequality metrics
metrics_long <- all_metrics %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Gini, Palma, S80_S20),
    names_to = "Measure",
    values_to = "Value"
  )
```

::: {.r-stack}

```{r}
#| label: fakeDist

ggplot(income_df, aes(x = Income)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) + # Use log scale for better visualization
  labs(
    x = "Income (Log Scale)",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Simulated Income Distributions"
  ) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(Society))
```

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
#| label: fakeStats

ggplot(metrics_long, aes(x = Measure, y = Value, color = Society)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Measure, ncol = 3, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    x = "Inequality Measure",
    y = "Calculated Value",
    title = "Simulated Indicators of Economic inequality"
  ) +
  scale_color_gb() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

:::

The measures agree on the ranking here because the simulation is clean. Real distributions rarely are.

:::

## Ready for the real world?

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_swiid.png){fig-align="center" height=600}


::: {.notes}

- 0.4 Gini: the richest 40% control about 60~70% of the fortune
- 0.6 Gini: the richest 20~30% control about 70~80%
- China's Gini has stayed above 0.4 since 2000, through SOE layoffs, the financial crisis, and COVID-19.

:::

## What people see is not what the data say

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_china_trust.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=600}

::: {.notes}

Objective and perceived inequality move apart, and it is the perceived one that travels with political trust. This is the first hint that the story is cognitive, not merely economic.

:::

## Why don't people ask for more?

What we have known: *inequality is bad for minds and for the social fabric* [@Cozzolino2011; @PayneEtAl2017; @Solt2008]

- Why don't citizens in unequal societies demand more redistribution? [@BelguiseEtAl2025; @HoyMager2021; @Whyte2010]

::: {.r-hstack}

![Don't know/care [@Bottero2019] Source: Generated by ChatGPT](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_dontCare.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=350}

![Believe things will get better [@HirschmanRothschild1973;@AndersonSinger2008] Source: 《我的要求不算高》](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_tunnelEffect.jpg){.fragment fig-align="center" height=350}

:::

::: {.notes}

- Tunnel effect: seeing the next lane move gives you hope rather than anger, because you expect to move soon yourself.
- The social-volcano thesis [@He2003a] predicts the opposite: inequality [&uarr;]{.blue} → unrest [&uarr;]{.blue} → stability [&darr;]{.red}. The volcano has stayed dormant.

:::

## My answer

:::: {.overlay-container}

::: {.overlay-text}

Both standard answers appear limited when:

- the economy *develops slower*, so the wall is no longer hidden, and
- people *come to know*, so exposure is no longer optional.

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_wallCollapse.webp){.fragment fig-align="center" height=450}

:::

::: {.overlay-text-over .fragment}

The economic environment changes minds &rarr; mass [indifference, even conservatism]{.red}, in redistribution preferences.

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

This is the thesis of the talk. The rest of the slides build it in two steps and one test:

1. *How*: the environment reshapes class consciousness and meritocratic belief (US).
2. *When/why*: it travels through perceptions of the closest institution (China).
3. *What if*: forcing people to compare still does not produce uniform demand for redistribution.

:::


# How

How does the economic environment reshape your beliefs about your own society?

## Economic inequality &rarr; social role

:::: {.overlay-container}

::: {.overlay-image}

::: {.r-hstack}

![Source: Reddit·r/AutisticUnion](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_classConsciousness.webp){.fragment fig-align="center" height=500}

![Source: *Zootopia* (2016)](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/mod_zootopia.gif){.fragment fig-align="center" height=500}

:::

:::

::: {.overlay-text-over .fragment}

- **Conflict theory**: under high inequality, the poor have *higher* class consciousness and believe in meritocracy [less]{.red}.
- **Relative power theory**: under high inequality, the poor do *not* gain class consciousness, and may believe in meritocracy [more]{.blue}.

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

- Class: bourgeoisie /bou-zhua-zi/, proletariat
- Meritocracy is the key to the American Dream and the hope of the poor
    - Self-reinforcing: relative power theory
    - Self-negating: conflict theory
- The stake is how a society reproduces itself.
- photo sources
    - https://www.reddit.com/r/AutisticUnion/comments/1dy10wo/what_was_youre_class_consciousness_moment/
    - https://sipofstarrshine.com/2016/03/15/zootopia-2016/

:::

## Examining the U.S. case

*Data*: [Pew survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/), national data of the U.S. (1999--2012)

$$
\begin{align}
\color{red}{Reject}\thinspace Meritocracy_{ij} =\boldsymbol{X\gamma} &+ \gamma_{10}Income_{ij} + \gamma_{01}Inequality_{j}\\
        &+ \gamma_{11}Inequality_{j} \times Income_{ij} + u_{ij}.
\end{align}
$$

::: {.r-hstack}

![@SoltEtAl2016](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_class1.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=300}

![@SoltEtAl2017](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/mod_SH_plot2.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=300}

:::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}

## Take-away

Higher inequality &rarr; *less* class-conscious and *more* attached to meritocracy

:::

::: {.notes}

Self-negating vs. self-reproducing. Relative power theory gets the support:

1. Economic inequality [reduces]{.red} people's class consciousness
1. Economic inequality [raises]{.blue} the poor's belief in meritocracy

Have-nots [@NewmanEtAl2015]: "Some people think of American society as divided into two groups, the 'haves' and the 'have-nots,' while others think it's incorrect to think of America that way. Do you, yourself, think of America as divided into haves and have-nots, or don't you think of America that way?"

The exact survey item and the marginal-effect plots are in the appendix.

:::


# When (why)

Through what channels does the macro environment reach the micro mind?

## From "what is" to "what should be"

**Perceiving** ahead of **judging**: if inequality reshapes minds, it likely does so through *evaluation*, not bare awareness [@KrieckhausEtAl2014]

![Source: China Value Survey (2021)](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_factPerceive.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height="450"}

::: {.notes}

- 贵港：广西壮族自治区
- 扬州/南京：江苏
- 抚州：江西省

People living under nearly identical Gini levels report very different perceptions.

:::

## People can feel inequality in *various* ways [@JinEtAl2024]

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.r-vstack}

![Impartial governance](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_collusion.jpg){fig-align="center" height=250}

![Government Non-responsiveness](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_nonresponse.jpg){.fragment fig-align="center" height=250}

:::

::: {.notes}

Impartial governance:

- The damage of economic disparities on political equality in democracies has been well documented in the literature [@SchlozmanEtAl2013].
- Formal and informal institutions exist in non-democracies to convert economic resources into political influence and favorable treatment.
- Wealthy Chinese private entrepreneurs form extensive connections with local government officials to gain privileges [@ChenDickson2010].

Government Non-responsiveness:

- Substantial evidence indicates that economic inequality reduces social capital and generates distrust and social conflicts.
- Class conflict theory suggests that in highly unequal societies, people's perceptions of economic positions on the social ladder are accentuated [@KrausEtAl2013].
- Low levels of social capital and accentuated social conflicts make governance difficult as @BaldwinHuber2010 showed that income differences make an agreement over which public goods to provide more difficult, therefore have a negative relationship with public goods provision [@EppJennings2020].

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.r-vstack}

![Judicial Injustice](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_judicialInjustice.jpg){.fragment fig-align="center" height=250}

![Anti-Corruption Inadequacy](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_anticorruption.jpg){.fragment fig-align="center" height=250}

:::

::: {.notes}

Judicial Injustice:

1. greater inequality implies that the well-off have more resources to control the legal apparatus while the poor are more disadvantaged.
1. the advantaged are motivated to attempt such control because of intensified social conflicts.

The Chinese classic case: 《葫芦僧判断葫芦案》, where the magistrate follows the "protective charm" list of the four great families instead of the law.

Anti-Corruption Inadequacy:

When inequality leads to widespread corruption, citizens doubt governments' intentions and abilities to combat corruption and perceive governments as incompetent to address the problems of the system.

人言包相是铁面，却原来官官相护有牵连

- photo links:
    - https://ncnewsline.com/2020/04/27/scales-of-injustice/

:::

:::

# What if

What happens when the wall comes down, when people are *forced* to compare?

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_wallCollapse.webp){fig-align="center" height=380}

## Comparison &rarr; Perception

> There exists, in the human organism, a drive to evaluate his opinions and abilities. The person will do this by [comparing himself with others]{.red}. [@Festinger1954, p. 117]

::: {.fragment}

- Upward comparison (vs. the rich) &rarr; discontent [@Crosby1976; @Gurr2015]
- Downward comparison (vs. the poor) &rarr; self-esteem [@Wills1981; @HopkinsBilimoria2008; @GibbonsGerrard1989]

::: {.callout-note .fragment}

## Comparison Effects

$H_{1.1}$: Upward comparison &rarr; redistribution support [&uarr;]{.red}

$H_{1.2}$: Downward comparison &rarr; redistribution support [&darr;]{.green}

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

The four-worlds view holds that people simply do not compare across strata. Urbanization and social media make the walls thinner. What follows when comparison becomes unavoidable?

:::

## Experimental Design [Inspired by @CondonWichowsky2020]

:::: {.overlay-container}

::: {.overlay-text}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

> [In Chinese] Given the social ladder on the left, please imagine the individuals in Chinese society who are the [(worst/best) off, (level 1/10)]{.red}, those who have the (least/most) wealth, (lowest/highest) education level, and (least respected/most respected) jobs. Specifically, [consider how you differ from these individuals]{.red} in terms of your own income, educational background, and job status.

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/macArthorLadder.jpg){fig-align="center" height=600}

:::

::::

:::

::: {.overlay-text-over .fragment}

Policy preferences:

Which of the following policies can help alleviate social and economic inequality and promote common prosperity?
Please rank the policies below **in order of importance** (You don't have to select all):

_______ Increasing the minimum living allowance (Dibao)<br>
_______ Raising retirement pensions<br>
_______ Raising unemployment benefits<br>
_______ Increasing the amount of education loans

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Data: China Value Survey (2021), nationally quota-representative, N = 3,603.

Participants in the control group are asked to imagine conversing with individuals who have similar income, education levels, and social status as themselves, and to reflect on what topics might arise in such a conversation.

:::

## Social comparison does "not" make a difference

::: {.r-stack}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_p2.png){fig-align="center" height=600}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_compare_unit.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=600}

:::

::: {.notes}

No significant effects, but the estimates run in the hypothesized direction. Post-experimental adjustment: sex, age, education, urban/rural, marital status, party membership; GDP, GDP growth, population, city-level Gini; provincial fixed effects.

:::

## Two explanations

::: {.r-stack}

!["How do you feel about the partner in the imagined conversation"](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_self.png){fig-align="center" height=600}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_result_expectation.jpg){.fragment fig-align="center" height=600}

![](https://drhuyue.site:10002/sammo3182/figure/inequality_result_policy.png){.fragment fig-align="center" height=600}

:::

::: {.notes}

Explanation 1, self vs. others: no one is worse off than the person standing where I stand. 没有比处于自己位置的人更苦的了。

Explanation 2, insider vs. outsider:

1. Among governmental employees, the lower-income ones report more fairness and higher expected mobility; the higher-income ones do not.
2. SOE employees voice policy demands, but mostly for policies benefiting people like themselves.
3. The masses do not think much further.

<!-- [Suggest] A 2x2 diagram crossing comparison direction with institutional position would make the two explanations land in one image -->

:::

## Take-home points

- **What** environment: an economic fact, but one that people read through sociopolitical lenses
- **How** it works: it reshapes beliefs about dreams and about power
- **What if** the wall falls: comparison alone does not move preferences, because institutions sort who feels what

::: {.callout-tip .fragment}

## Psychological health tips

[Knowing]{.red} what you feel about inequality, [learning]{.red} why you feel so, and [leading]{.red} how you feel

:::


[*The cognitive factors nested in institutional structures keep the "social volcano" dormant, but people are [neither unaware nor indifferent]{.red}.*]{.large .fragment}


::: {.notes}

Open questions: alternative explanations for the "what if" findings; what governments can do; the role of communication technology in this process.

:::

\end{align}

## Marginal Effects on Class Consciousness and Meritocracy

::: {.r-hstack}

## Examining on the China Case

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

Data:

*Chinese Household Finance Survey* (CHFS) 2013

+ 28,141 households from 29 provinces
+ Representative income data for Gini coefficient

*China Urban Governance Survey* (CUGS) 2015

+ 3,513 from 50 prefectures
+ Later than CHFS
+ Political perceptions

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Measurement:

- Governance &rarr; Perceptions of government equality in treating citizens
- Responsiveness &larr; External political efficacy
- Justice &larr; Trust in the courts' and procuratorates' fairness
- Anti-corruption &larr; Satisfaction of anti-corruption

Method: *Causal mediation analysis*

+ Multi-mediator estimation
+ central and local governments

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

Imai 2014, mediation analysis for causal mechanism and non-binary treatment

:::

## Measurement of Social Comparison (CVS 2021, N = 3,603)

:::{.r-stack}

- Outcome
    - Inequality perception: income distribution fairness (1--4)
    - Preference in redistribution policies
        - Minimum subsistence allowance (*dibao*) &larr; benefit the [poor]{.green}
        - Unemployment insurance &larr; benefit the [poor]{.green}
        - Education loans &larr; benefit the [middle]{.blue}/[poor]{.green}
        - Pension &larr; benefit the [middle]{.blue}/[rich]{.red}
- Income: Low-middle-high ([official categorization](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202102/t20210228_1814177.html))
- Co-optation: governmental or SOE employed
- Control:
    - Gender, age, education, urban/rural, party member
    - GDP, GDP growth rate, population, city-level Gini

:::

::: {.notes}

the per capita disposable income of low-income group reached 7,869 yuan, the lower-middle-income group 16,443 yuan, the middle-income group 26,249 yuan, the upper-middle-income group 41,172 yuan and the high-income group 80,294 yuan.

:::

::: {.notes}

Being in the danwei reduces low-income people's support of dibao and pension under upward comparison, and raises their support of unemployment insurance under downward comparison.

Being in the danwei, both upward and downward comparison increase the middle class's support of dibao.

Being in the danwei reduces high-income earners' support of dibao and increases their support of pension.

:::
